explain.say: Not all rain runs into rivers. Much of it soaks into the ground and trickles down through soil and cracks in rock. This hidden water is called groundwater.

explain.say: Rock that holds lots of water and lets it flow, like sandstone or chalk, is called an aquifer. It is not an underground lake but rock soaked like a sponge.

explain.say: Below lies clay or solid rock that water cannot pass through, so the water collects above it. Groundwater moves slowly, often just centimetres a day, and wells and springs tap into it.

faq.a: The water table is the level underground below which every gap in the soil and rock is full of water. It rises after wet seasons and falls in droughts or when too much water is pumped out.
An aquifer is a layer of rock, sand or gravel that holds lots of water in its pores and cracks and lets it flow. Wells drilled into aquifers supply drinking water.

faq.q: How much fresh water is groundwater?
faq.a: About 30 percent of Earth's fresh water is groundwater, far more than all the lakes and rivers. Most of the rest is frozen in ice caps and glaciers.
Usually very slowly, from a few centimetres to a metre or so a day, so water can stay underground for years, centuries or even thousands of years.
Yes. If people pump it out faster than rain refills it, the water table falls and wells can run dry. Parts of some big aquifers, like the Ogallala in the United States, are being drained.
asks: What happens if we pump too much groundwater?

facts: About 30 percent of Earth's fresh water is groundwater.
Groundwater supplies about half of the drinking water used around the world.

quiz.why: An aquifer is porous rock, sand or gravel soaked with water that can flow through it to wells and springs.

wrong.1: Lava is molten rock, nothing to do with groundwater.
